topic: Secondary prevention after acute coronary syndrome

audits.title: Prescription of secondary prevention medications, lifestyle advice, and referral to rehabilitation among acute coronary syndrome inpatients: results from a large prospective audit in Australia and New Zealand.
audits.standard: Optimal in-hospital preventive care: lifestyle advice, rehabilitation referral and secondary prevention medicines
audits.setting: All hospitals admitting ACS patients in Australia and New Zealand

cycle1.result: 46% referred to rehabilitation, 65% discharged on sufficient preventive medicines, 27% received optimal preventive care.

audits.other_findings: Unstable angina, no PCI, age over 70 and private hospital admission were linked to less optimal care.
audits.citation: Redfern J, Hyun K, Chew DP, Astley C, Chow C, Aliprandi-Costa B, et al.. Prescription of secondary prevention medications, lifestyle advice, and referral to rehabilitation among acute coronary syndrome inpatients: results from a large prospective audit in Australia and New Zealand. Heart. 2014;100(16):1281-1288. doi:10.1136/heartjnl-2013-305296. PMID: 24914060.

audits.title: Secondary prevention following myocardial infarction: evidence from an audit in South Wales that the National Service Framework for coronary heart disease does not address all the issues.
audits.standard: National Service Framework for coronary heart disease: 80-90% prescribed appropriate secondary prevention by April 2002
audits.setting: Teaching hospital and community, Llandough Hospital, Cardiff

cycle1.result: At discharge, unless contraindicated: aspirin 100%, beta-blockers 84%, statin and/or dietetic advice 66%, ACE inhibitors in heart failure 97%.

audits.other_findings: At 1-2 years, cholesterol remained above 5.0 mmol/l in 25%, 24% had stopped beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors stayed at low dose in half.
audits.citation: Underwood P, Beck P. Secondary prevention following myocardial infarction: evidence from an audit in South Wales that the National Service Framework for coronary heart disease does not address all the issues. Qual Saf Health Care. 2002;11(3):230-232. doi:10.1136/qhc.11.3.230. PMID: 12486986.

audits.title: Current discharge management of acute coronary syndromes: baseline results from a national quality improvement initiative.
audits.standard: National guidelines for ACS discharge medications, cardiac rehabilitation referral and discharge communication

cycle1.result: 57% prescribed antiplatelet, beta-blocker, statin and ACE inhibitor/ARB at discharge; 83% had a documented ACS management plan.

audits.other_findings: Baseline audit; 67% recalled cardiac rehabilitation referral, of whom 33% completed; 48% on the combination at 3 months.
audits.citation: Wai A, Pulver LK, Oliver K, Thompson A. Current discharge management of acute coronary syndromes: baseline results from a national quality improvement initiative. Intern Med J. 2012;42(5):e53-9. doi:10.1111/j.1445-5994.2010.02308.x. PMID: 20646093.

audits.title: Management of acute coronary syndromes at hospital discharge: do targeted educational interventions improve practice quality?
audits.standard: Evidence-based ACS guidelines (discharge medications, cardiac rehabilitation referral, communication)

cycle1.result: All four recommended medications 57%; short-acting nitrates 56%; cardiac rehabilitation referral 57%.

audits.intervention: Educational meetings, academic detailing, point-of-care reminders and feedback of baseline results.

cycle2.result: All four medications 69%; nitrates 68%; cardiac rehabilitation referral 68% (all p<.0001).

audits.other_findings: Discharge medication counselling, smoking cessation counselling and management plan communication also increased significantly.
audits.citation: Peterson GM, Thompson A, Pulver LK, Robertson MB, Brieger D, Wai A, et al.. Management of acute coronary syndromes at hospital discharge: do targeted educational interventions improve practice quality?. J Healthc Qual. 2012;34(1):26-34. doi:10.1111/j.1945-1474.2011.00137.x. PMID: 22059443.

audits.title: Use of evidence-based therapy at discharge for patients with acute myocardial infarction: retrospective audit of medical records.
audits.standard: Canadian benchmarks: ASA at least 90%, beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors at least 85%, statins at least 70%
audits.setting: Single health authority, Newfoundland and Labrador

cycle1.result: In ideal patients: ASA 99.0% (308/311), beta-blockers 96.3% (310/322), ACE inhibitors 90.4% (264/292), statins 88.8% (278/313); all exceeded benchmarks.

audits.citation: Young SW, Hawboldt JJ, Pearce NJ. Use of evidence-based therapy at discharge for patients with acute myocardial infarction: retrospective audit of medical records. Can J Hosp Pharm. 2010;63(3):207-211. doi:10.4212/cjhp.v63i3.916. PMID: 22478980.

audits.title: Findings from a clinical audit in regional general practice of management of patients following acute coronary syndrome.
audits.standard: National Heart Foundation guidelines for acute coronary syndrome
audits.setting: 22 GPs in a regional centre, Western Australia; general practice

cycle1.result: 90% (n=39) of discharge summaries recorded medications; 53% (n=23) received four or more drug classes; 87% (13 of 15) of smokers had quit advice; 30% (n=13) referred to a dietitian; 25% (n=10) referred to cardiac rehabilitation.

audits.other_findings: Diet and exercise advice was poorly documented; 18 (41%) were diagnosed depressed, 88% started antidepressants, and patients with type 2 diabetes were more likely to get allied health referral.
audits.citation: Dronavalli M, Bhagwat MM, Hamilton S, Gilles M, Garton-Smith J, Thompson SC. Findings from a clinical audit in regional general practice of management of patients following acute coronary syndrome. Aust J Prim Health. 2017;23(2):170-177. doi:10.1071/py15191. PMID: 27647550.

audits.title: Optimal dosing of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and β-blockers for acute coronary syndrome: up-titration remains a challenge.
audits.standard: NICE guidelines: prompt initiation and up-titration of ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers after acute coronary syndrome
audits.setting: Leeds General Infirmary, Leeds (inpatient and community)

cycle1.result: Inpatient up-titration of bisoprolol and ramipril, discharge advice and doses at 6 weeks after discharge assessed (baseline figures not reported).

audits.intervention: Multidisciplinary education, posters and discharge advice templates.

cycle2.result: Significant improvement in mean difference from initiation to discharge dose for ramipril (p=0.012) and bisoprolol (p=0.017); 68% improvement in discharge advice.

audits.other_findings: Community up-titration after discharge showed little difference despite better discharge advice.
audits.citation: Sharma N, Khatib R, Elamin N, Eaden J, Choong CE, Jones C, et al.. Optimal dosing of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and β-blockers for acute coronary syndrome: up-titration remains a challenge. Eur J Hosp Pharm. 2016;23(4):203-206. doi:10.1136/ejhpharm-2015-000783. PMID: 31156849.

audits.title: Implementation of clinical audit to improve adherence to guideline-recommended therapy in acute coronary syndrome.
audits.standard: Guideline-directed medical therapy at discharge (statins, dual antiplatelet therapy, beta-blockers, ACE-I/ARB) with no unjustifiable omissions
audits.setting: Department of Cardiology, PSG Institute of Medical Sciences and Research, Coimbatore

cycle1.result: Unreasonable omissions in first month: DAPT 1%, statin 0%, ACE-I/ARB 14%, beta-blockers 11%.

audits.intervention: Clinical pharmacist-led monthly audit with feedback report presented to cardiologists.

cycle2.result: Unreasonable omissions reduced to nil by the end of the 11th month and stayed nil to the 12th month.

audits.other_findings: 1072 is the total audited over 12 months; improvement sustained to month 12.
audits.citation: George NE, Shukkoor AA, Joseph N, Palanimuthu R, Kaliappan T, Gopalan R. Implementation of clinical audit to improve adherence to guideline-recommended therapy in acute coronary syndrome. Egypt Heart J. 2022;74(1):4. doi:10.1186/s43044-021-00237-7. PMID: 35020077.

audits.title: Management of hyperlipidaemia following acute coronary syndrome: a retrospective audit.
audits.standard: NICE recommendations on PCSK9 inhibitor eligibility after ACS and repeat lipid measurement
audits.setting: Two cardiac centres in the West Midlands (Worcester Royal Hospital and Royal Stoke University Hospital)

cycle1.result: LDL measured on admission in 93 and repeated within three months in 20 (13%); 48 (30%) had any repeat LDL; 10 met NICE criteria for PCSK9i.

audits.other_findings: Underreporting of polyvascular disease also limited identification of very high-risk patients.
audits.citation: Salim HY, Lwin K, Khoo C, Wilson D. Management of hyperlipidaemia following acute coronary syndrome: a retrospective audit. Br J Cardiol. 2021;28(2):17. doi:10.5837/bjc.2021.017. PMID: 35747451.

audits.title: Secondary prevention lipid management after ACS at a DGH: a quality improvement project.
audits.standard: Guideline-based post-ACS lipid management: inpatient lipid profile, inpatient lipid-lowering therapy management and outpatient repeat lipid profile
audits.setting: District general hospital (Wiltshire Cardiac Centre, Great Western Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Swindon)

cycle1.result: Baseline full lipid profile testing 10%; appropriate LLT management 65%; post-discharge repeat testing 37%

audits.intervention: Structured intervention including updated blood testing panels, education and reference resources

cycle2.result: Full lipid profile testing 75%; appropriate LLT management 78%; post-discharge repeat testing 63%

audits.other_findings: At one year post-ACS, 35% of patients remained subtherapeutic but medication changes were rare.
audits.citation: Laird M, Tang PT, Patel M, Hyde T. Secondary prevention lipid management after ACS at a DGH: a quality improvement project. Br J Cardiol. 2026;33(3):035. doi:10.5837/bjc.2026.035. PMID: 42719811.

audits.title: An audit of lipid screening and management in patients undergoing diagnostic cardiac catheterization. Brompton House Officer Audit Group.
audits.standard: Target lipid levels in coronary artery disease
audits.setting: Diagnostic cardiac catheterisation patients, Royal Brompton Hospital, London

cycle1.result: Lipid result documented in 46/206 (22%); 169/206 (82%) total cholesterol > 5.2; only 22 (11%) on drug therapy; most treated patients not at target.

audits.other_findings: Low HDL and high TC/HDL ratio were associated with disease presence and extent.
audits.citation: Stables RH, Choudhury RP, Davies WG, Denton MD, Ledson M, Rakhit RD, et al.. An audit of lipid screening and management in patients undergoing diagnostic cardiac catheterization. Brompton House Officer Audit Group. Eur Heart J. 1996;17(11):1657-1662. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.eurheartj.a014748. PMID: 8922913.

audits.title: An audit of discharge medication for secondary prophylaxis post-myocardial infarction.
audits.standard: Discharge standard for secondary prophylaxis post-MI

cycle1.result: 39 of 60 (65%) met the discharge standard; no significant difference between cardiologist-led and general medical teams.

audits.intervention: Guidelines developed feeding into the cardiac rehabilitation programme; follow-up audit planned.
audits.other_findings: Highlighted dilemma of adding low-dose aspirin for patients on warfarin.
audits.citation: Richardson J, Truman C. An audit of discharge medication for secondary prophylaxis post-myocardial infarction. J Clin Pharm Ther. 1996;21(6):413-416. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2710.1996.tb00040.x. PMID: 9201568.
